newsitem.title: INDIA: India IPCL may invest in power, refinery.
newsitem.headline: India IPCL may invest in power, refinery.

text.p: State-run Indian Petrochemicals Corporation (IPCL) is considering diversifying into refinery and power industries, its chairman said on Wednesday.

"The company is also considering to invest in refinery and power plants to mitigate the cyclic trends of petrochemical business," K.G. Ramanathan told a shareholders meeting in the western city of Vadodara.
He did not elaborate on plans in these sectors. IPCL is India's leading integrated petrochemicals producer.
He said IPCL was evaluating capital investment proposals valued at 60 billion rupees spread over the next few years.
This will include a 100,000 tonnes per year acrylonitrile plant at Dahej on the western coast, for which technology licensing agreement was signed BP Chemicals of U.K.
Acrylonitrile is the raw material for acrylic fibre.
Ramanathan said IPCL commissioned some sections of a new 75,000 tonnes per year polypropylene plant and 30,000 tonnes a year polybutadiene rubber plant at Vadodara.

"We expect these two plants to go on stream very soon. The work on expansion of gas cracker, high density polyethylene and linear low density polyethylene at Nagothane is going on as per schedule and we plan to make them operational by end 1997."
The first phase of IPCL's third petrochemical complex at Gandhar, consisting of a PVC plant, a dedicated power plant and a jetty, is expected to be commissioned soon, he said.
IPCL's existing petrochemical complexes are in Vadodara and Nagothane, both in western India.
IPCL is connecting its upcoming Gandhar complex with the older Vadodara plant through three pipelines -- one each for naphtha, ethylene and propylene, Ramanathan said.
The jetty at Dahej near Gandhar will also be used for importing raw materials like naphtha, he said.
"Our expansion plans will contribute to the economies of scale and enable us to maintain the market share in the growing domestic market," the chairman told shareholders.
He said international polymer prices continued to be depressed. A reduction in customs duties in the government's July budget has not helped Indian producers, Ramanathan said.
"The lowering of prices, coupled with the recent hike in the administered prices of naphtha and other petroleum feedstock affected our margins," Ramanathan said.
"We have made representations to the government on all these factors so that long-term viability of the domestic petrochemical industry is not adversely affected," he said.
